settings.markdown:
Lessons

Example lessons for Grade 8 US History. Each one pairs a MapMaker map with an inquiry, a Word student sheet in English and Spanish, and teacher notes.

Drafts: not yet reviewed 5 lessons · US History

• October

    1775–1776 Revolutionary Battles

    US History · Grade 8 · Road to revolution and the Revolution

    Explore how the geography of North America shaped the first two years of the American Revolution, from the first shots at Lexington and Concord to Washington's attack on Trenton.

    Draft: not yet reviewed

  • February

    Roads, Trails, and Rails West

    US History · Grade 8 · Westward expansion and Manifest Destiny

    Follow the trails settlers took west in the 1800s, see whose lands they crossed, and find out how railroads replaced the wagon trails.

    Draft: not yet reviewed

  • March

    US Slavery and Slave Trade, 1850

    US History · Grade 8 · Reform and the road to war

    Compare free and slave states in 1850, follow the routes of the internal slave trade south, and trace the Underground Railroad north to freedom.

    Draft: not yet reviewed

  • April

    Civil War Battlefields

    US History · Grade 8 · The Civil War

    See how the United States split in 1861, compare the railroads of the North and the South, and find where the war's battles were fought.

    Draft: not yet reviewed

  • April

    The Battle of Vicksburg

    US History · Grade 8 · The Civil War

    Follow Grant's 1863 march to Vicksburg along the Mississippi River, and see why taking the city split the Confederacy in two.

    Draft: not yet reviewed

In every lesson

  • A MapMaker map that opens straight from the page, with each layer’s source listed.
  • An inquiry with a compelling question and questions you can pick from.
  • A Word student sheet in English and Spanish that you can edit, print or open in Google Docs.
  • Teacher notes with answers, common misunderstandings, key words and standards.
  • Links to how-to videos, and to Vera for making your own questions.

pages.summary: Explore how the geography of North America shaped the first two years of the American Revolution, from the first shots at Lexington and Concord to Washington's attack on Trenton.

settings.markdown:
Lessons › US History

1775–1776 Revolutionary Battles

Explore how the geography of North America shaped the first two years of the American Revolution, from the first shots at Lexington and Concord to Washington's attack on Trenton.

  • Grade8
  • Time45 minutes, or 10–15 per question
  • UnitRoad to revolution and the Revolution
  • Student loginNot needed to explore the map

Open in MapMaker (opens in a new tab) Student sheet (Word, English) Hoja del estudiante (Word, español)

Draft: not yet reviewed Content version 0.2.1, updated 2026-10-12.

About this map

Each layer names its source, so you can check where the information comes from.

LayerWhat it showsSource
Revolutionary War BattlesWhat it shows: 21 battles from April 1775 to December 1776. Each pop-up gives the dates, a picture and a short account of the battle. The symbol color shows the winner, as listed in the legend (American victory or British victory).Source: American Battlefield Trust
Revolutionary War BattlefieldsWhat it shows: Battlefield boundaries, and the core areas where the fighting was heaviestSource: National Park Service, American Battlefield Protection Program
Turning PointsWhat it shows: Five events, from Lexington and Concord to Trenton, with short notesSource: Chris Bunin and Peter Trentacoste (2026), from National Park Service, US Army Center of Military History and Library of Congress sources
Thirteen British ColoniesWhat it shows: Colony borders in 1763Source: National Geographic Society and Virginia Geographic Alliance, from the Historical Atlas of the United States (1988)
1763 Proclamation LineWhat it shows: The line west of which King George III barred colonial settlementSource: National Geographic Society and Virginia Geographic Alliance, from the Historical Atlas of the United States (1988)
Key Port Cities in the American Revolution 1775-1781 (off when the map opens)What it shows: Ports that supplied armies and moved troopsSource: Jay Feyerabend, master's thesis (opens in a new tab), James Madison University (2021)

Bookmarks: Massachusetts.

Known issues

No known issues.

Inquiry

Compelling question

Why did the fighting move from Boston to New York, and then across New Jersey, in 1775–1776?

Pick the questions that suit your class. Each one lists the MapMaker tools it uses, linked to how-to videos.

  1. Where did the war begin?

    Open the Massachusetts bookmark and click Lexington and Concord, then Boston. Note the dates, and the winner from the symbol color and legend. Measure the straight-line distance from Boston to Concord.

    Tools: Bookmarks, how-to video: Navigating MapMaker (opens in a new tab) · Pop-ups, how-to video: Explore Layers and Data (opens in a new tab) · Legend, how-to video: Explore Layers and Data (opens in a new tab) · Measure, how-to video: Measure with MapMaker (opens in a new tab)

  2. Where was the fighting in 1775, and where in 1776?

    Click the battles and sort them into two lists by year. Which colonies saw fighting each year, and what changed?

    Tools: Pop-ups, how-to video: Explore Layers and Data (opens in a new tab) · Legend, how-to video: Explore Layers and Data (opens in a new tab)

  3. Why New York?

    Turn on Key Port Cities and zoom to New York. Compare its harbor and rivers with Boston's. What could a navy do from New York?

    Tools: Map layers, how-to video: Explore Layers and Data (opens in a new tab) · Zoom, how-to video: Navigating MapMaker (opens in a new tab)

  4. How did 1776 end?

    Find Fort Washington, Fort Lee and Trenton, and note who won each. Measure the distance from New York City to Trenton.

    Tools: Pop-ups, how-to video: Explore Layers and Data (opens in a new tab) · Measure, how-to video: Measure with MapMaker (opens in a new tab)

Answering the compelling question

Students answer with evidence from at least two places on the map. Some ways to do it: a paragraph, a route drawn with Sketch, or bookmarks saved for a short talk.

Tools: Sketch, how-to video: Sketch on a Map (opens in a new tab) · Bookmarks, how-to video: Navigating MapMaker (opens in a new tab)

Student activity

This is what students see on the Word sheet. Download it to edit it, print it, or open it in Google Docs.

Download Word (English) Download Word (Español)

1775–1776 Revolutionary Battles

Student sheet

Name Date

Big question: Why did the fighting move from Boston to New York, and then across New Jersey, in 1775–1776?

Open the map in MapMaker: 1775–1776 Revolutionary Battles

  1. Where did the war begin? Open the Massachusetts bookmark. Click Lexington and Concord. When was it fought? Use the legend to find out who won. Measure the straight-line distance from Boston to Concord: miles
  2. Where was the fighting in 1775, and where in 1776? Click the battles and sort them by year. Which colonies had battles in 1775? Which in 1776? What changed?
  3. Why New York? Turn on Key Port Cities and zoom to New York. Compare its harbor and rivers with Boston's. What could a navy do from New York?
  4. How did 1776 end? Find Fort Washington, Fort Lee and Trenton. Who won each? Measure the distance from New York City to Trenton: miles

Your answer: Answer the big question using evidence from at least two places on the map. You can write a paragraph, sketch on the map, or both.

Español: Spanish draft for review by a native speaker. Layer names stay in English, as they appear in MapMaker.

Teacher notes

Before class

No preparation beyond checking the map opens on student devices. Students don't need accounts to explore it; saving their own copy needs a sign-in.

Answer notes

1. Where did the war begin?

Lexington and Concord, April 19, 1775, an American victory. The siege of Boston ran from April 19, 1775, to March 17, 1776. Boston to Concord is about 16 miles (26 km) in a straight line, so expect answers of 15–17 miles.

2. Where was the fighting in 1775, and where in 1776?

YearAmerican victoriesBritish victories
1775 (8 battles)American victories: Lexington and Concord, Boston (siege) and Gloucester (Massachusetts); Fort Ticonderoga and Crown Point (New York); Great Bridge (Virginia)British victories: Bunker Hill (Massachusetts); Quebec (Quebec)
1776 (13 battles)American victories: Moores Creek Bridge (North Carolina); Sullivan's Island and Breach Inlet (South Carolina); Gwynn's Island (Virginia); Trenton (New Jersey)British victories: Brooklyn, Valcour Island, Pell's Point, White Plains, Fort Washington (New York); Fort Lee, Mount Holly (New Jersey); Newport (Rhode Island)

Fighting began around Boston, then spread along the coast. From August 1776 most battles were in New York and New Jersey.

3. Why New York?

The American Battlefield Trust says the city's "central position in the American Colonies and its port made it vital to commerce and a key strategic location", and that British warships could "dominate the river waterways that cut through New York City." The British left Boston in March 1776 and won at Brooklyn on August 27. (Battle of Brooklyn, American Battlefield Trust (opens in a new tab))

4. How did 1776 end?

Fort Washington (November 16) and Fort Lee (November 20) were British victories; Trenton (December 26) was an American victory. New York City to Trenton is about 52 miles (84 km) in a straight line.

Common misunderstandings

  • “The early war was fought in Massachusetts.” By the end of 1776 the map shows battles in seven colonies and in Quebec.
  • “The winner is the side that lost fewer soldiers.” Bunker Hill is shown as a British victory, yet its pop-up says the British had twice as many casualties as the Patriots.
  • “The Americans lost every battle in 1776.” The map shows American wins in the South that year, such as Moores Creek Bridge and Sullivan's Island, as well as Trenton.

Key words

  • siege
  • militia
  • Continental Army
  • Loyalist
  • harbor
  • campaign
  • retreat

Standards

CodeStandard
TX 8.4(C)Standard: Explain the issues surrounding important events of the American Revolution, including declaring independence; fighting the battles of Lexington and Concord, Saratoga, and Yorktown; enduring the winter at Valley Forge; and signing the Treaty of Paris of 1783
TX 8.10(A)Standard: Locate places and regions directly related to major eras and turning points in the United States during the 17th, 18th, and 19th centuries
TX 8.10(C)Standard: Analyze the effects of physical and human geographic factors such as weather, landforms, waterways, transportation, and communication on major historical events in the United States
FL SS.8.A.3.6Standard: Examine the causes, course, and consequences of the American Revolution
C3 D2.Geo.2.6-8Standard: Use maps, satellite images, photographs, and other representations to explain relationships between the locations of places and regions, and changes in their environmental characteristics
C3 D2.His.14.6-8Standard: Explain multiple causes and effects of events and developments in the past

Draft list, to be checked against each state's current standards.

settings.markdown:
Lessons › US History

Roads, Trails, and Rails West

Follow the trails settlers took west in the 1800s, see whose lands they crossed, and find out how railroads replaced the wagon trails.

  • Grade8
  • Time45 minutes, or 10–15 per question
  • UnitWestward expansion and Manifest Destiny
  • Student loginNot needed to explore the map

Open in MapMaker (opens in a new tab) Student sheet (Word, English) Hoja del estudiante (Word, español)

Draft: not yet reviewed Content version 0.1.0, updated 2026-10-12.

About this map

Each layer names its source, so you can check where the information comes from.

LayerWhat it showsSource
Trails WestWhat it shows: Seven trails west: Oregon, California, Mormon Pioneer, Old Spanish, Santa Fe, Butterfield Overland and Pony Express, each in its own color in the legend. Each pop-up gives the trail's name and a short history with dates.Source: National Geographic Education, from National Park Service trail information
Transcontinental Railroads completed by 1911 (off when the map opens)What it shows: Five transcontinental lines named in the legend: Great Northern, Northern Pacific, Union Pacific, Central Pacific and Southern Pacific. No pop-up.Source: Jeremy Atack, historical railroad data (ICPSR 36353), prepared by the MapMaker team
Railroads 1826 to 1911 (off when the map opens)What it shows: Railroad lines built from 1826 to 1911. Each pop-up gives the year the line was in operation by.Source: Jeremy Atack, historical railroad data (ICPSR 36353), prepared by the MapMaker team
Indigenous Territories (off when the map opens)What it shows: Approximate territories of Indigenous nations, from a community-made map. No pop-up.Source: Native Land Digital

Bookmarks: none.

Known issues

  • Open 2026-10-12 Trails West pop-up (Oregon): Gives the years 1840 to 1860, then says many travelers were "fleeing the American Civil War (1861-1865)", which began after that period.

Inquiry

Compelling question

How did trails and then railroads change the American West, and for whom?

Pick the questions that suit your class. Each one lists the MapMaker tools it uses, linked to how-to videos.

  1. Where did the trails begin?

    Click three trails and note where each started and ended. Most began in Missouri: why there?

    Tools: Pop-ups, how-to video: Explore Layers and Data (opens in a new tab) · Legend, how-to video: Explore Layers and Data (opens in a new tab)

  2. How far, and how many?

    Open the Oregon Trail pop-up for its length and how many people used it. Measure the straight-line distance from Independence, Missouri, to Portland, Oregon, and compare it with the trail's length.

    Tools: Pop-ups, how-to video: Explore Layers and Data (opens in a new tab) · Measure, how-to video: Measure with MapMaker (opens in a new tab)

  3. Whose land?

    Turn on Indigenous Territories and follow one trail. Was the West empty land when the trails were built?

    Tools: Map layers, how-to video: Explore Layers and Data (opens in a new tab)

  4. From trails to rails

    Turn on the Railroads layers. Which trail does the first transcontinental line follow most closely? Click a railroad line to see when it was in operation.

    Tools: Map layers, how-to video: Explore Layers and Data (opens in a new tab) · Pop-ups, how-to video: Explore Layers and Data (opens in a new tab) · Legend, how-to video: Explore Layers and Data (opens in a new tab)

Answering the compelling question

Students answer with evidence from at least two layers. Some ways to do it: a paragraph, one journey sketched on the map with notes, or a short talk using the map.

Tools: Sketch, how-to video: Sketch on a Map (opens in a new tab)

Student activity

This is what students see on the Word sheet. Download it to edit it, print it, or open it in Google Docs.

Download Word (English) Download Word (Español)

Roads, Trails, and Rails West

Student sheet

Name Date

Big question: How did trails and then railroads change the American West, and for whom?

Open the map in MapMaker: Roads, Trails, and Rails West

  1. Where did the trails begin? Click three trails. Where did each one start and end? In which state do most of the trails start?
  2. How far, and how many? Click the Oregon Trail. How long was it, and how many people traveled it? Why is the trail longer than a straight line? Measure the straight-line distance from Independence, Missouri, to Portland, Oregon: miles
  3. Whose land? Turn on the Indigenous Territories layer and follow one trail. Was the land the trail crossed empty? What might the trail have meant for the people who lived there?
  4. From trails to rails Turn on the Railroads layers. Which trails does the Union Pacific and Central Pacific line follow most closely? Click a railroad line: when was it in operation?

Your answer: Answer the big question using evidence from at least two layers on the map. You can write a paragraph, sketch on the map, or both.

Español: Spanish draft for review by a native speaker. Layer names stay in English, as they appear in MapMaker.

Teacher notes

Before class

The Railroads and Indigenous Territories layers are off when the map opens; students turn them on in the layer list. The map has no bookmarks, so students zoom and pan to find places.

Answer notes

1. Where did the trails begin?

TrailFromTo
OregonFrom: Independence, MissouriTo: Willamette River valley, near Portland, Oregon
CaliforniaFrom: Independence, Missouri, and Omaha, NebraskaTo: Northern California
Mormon PioneerFrom: Near Omaha, NebraskaTo: Salt Lake City, Utah
Santa FeFrom: MissouriTo: Santa Fe, New Mexico
Pony ExpressFrom: St. Joseph, MissouriTo: Sacramento, California
Butterfield OverlandFrom: St. Louis, Missouri, and Memphis, Tennessee, via Fort Smith, ArkansasTo: San Francisco, California
Old SpanishFrom: Abiquiú, New MexicoTo: Los Angeles, California

Most start in Missouri, at the western edge of the settled states and on the Missouri River, where travelers could buy supplies before setting out.

2. How far, and how many?

The pop-up gives about 2,000 miles (3,219 km) and 300,000 to 400,000 people between 1840 and 1860. The straight line is about 1,500 miles (2,420 km). The trail is longer because it followed rivers for water and grass, and crossed the Rocky Mountains through passes.

3. Whose land?

No. The layer shows Indigenous nations' territories across all the land the trails crossed. The map's description notes that Manifest Destiny overlooked the Indigenous and Hispanic people already living in the West, and that trails and railways crossing Native lands led to conflict and great loss of land.

4. From trails to rails

It runs close to the California and Mormon Pioneer trails across Nebraska, Wyoming, Utah and Nevada. The first transcontinental railroad was completed in 1869, the year the California Trail pop-up says that trail's use ended. The Pony Express pop-up says it stopped in October 1861, when a transcontinental telegraph line was completed.

Common misunderstandings

  • “The West was empty before settlers arrived.” The Indigenous Territories layer shows nations' lands across the whole region the trails crossed.
  • “Everyone went west on the Oregon Trail.” The map shows seven trails, to Oregon, California, Utah, New Mexico and Southern California.
  • “The Pony Express lasted for decades.” Its pop-up says it ran for 18 months, from April 1860 to October 1861.

Key words

  • Manifest Destiny
  • emigrant
  • trail
  • transcontinental railroad
  • telegraph
  • Indigenous nation

Standards

CodeStandard
TX 8.6(B)Standard: Explain the political, economic, and social roots of Manifest Destiny
TX 8.6(C)Standard: Analyze the relationship between the concept of Manifest Destiny and the westward growth of the nation
TX 8.11(A)Standard: Analyze how physical characteristics of the environment influenced population distribution, settlement patterns, and economic activities in the United States during the 17th, 18th, and 19th centuries
FL SS.8.A.4.1Standard: Examine the causes, course, and consequences of United States westward expansion and its growing diplomatic assertiveness
C3 D2.Geo.7.6-8Standard: Explain how changes in transportation and communication technology influence the spatial connections among human settlements and affect the diffusion of ideas and cultural practices
C3 D2.His.14.6-8Standard: Explain multiple causes and effects of events and developments in the past

settings.markdown:
Lessons › US History

US Slavery and Slave Trade, 1850

Compare free and slave states in 1850, follow the routes of the internal slave trade south, and trace the Underground Railroad north to freedom.

  • Grade8
  • Time45 minutes, or 10–15 per question
  • UnitReform and the road to war
  • Student loginNot needed to explore the map

Open in MapMaker (opens in a new tab) Student sheet (Word, English) Hoja del estudiante (Word, español)

Draft: not yet reviewed Content version 0.1.0, updated 2026-10-12.

About this map

Each layer names its source, so you can check where the information comes from.

LayerWhat it showsSource
US States and Territories 1850What it shows: States and territories in four legend groups: free states, free by compromise, slave states, and slave by compromise. Each pop-up says whether the state or territory allowed slavery and from what year.Source: Traced from a map in Harper's Atlas of American History (1920), as the pop-ups say
Internal Routes of the US Slave TradeWhat it shows: Routes along which enslaved people were forced to move within the United States. No pop-up.Source: Traced from Harper's Atlas of American History (1920)
Underground Railroad Approximate RoutesWhat it shows: Approximate routes that freedom seekers took north to the free states and Canada. No pop-up.Source: Traced from Harper's Atlas of American History (1920), an early-1900s interpretation
CitiesWhat it shows: 69 towns and cities along the Underground Railroad routes, from Virginia and Kentucky to Ontario and Quebec. No pop-up.Source: Traced from Harper's Atlas of American History (1920)
Missouri Compromise LineWhat it shows: The line at 36°30′ North set in 1820: slavery was barred north of it in the Louisiana Territory, except in Missouri. No pop-up.Source: Not stated on the layer (hosted by the MapMaker team)
US 1850 Original Map (off when the map opens)What it shows: A scan of the 1850 map that the other layers were traced from. No pop-up.Source: Harper's Atlas of American History (1920)

Bookmarks: Illinois, Indiana, and Ohio.

Known issues

  • Open 2026-10-12 US States and Territories 1850 pop-up: The line "It is recorded on the primary source as:" shows a code number (for example 11) instead of the map's own wording.
  • Open 2026-10-12 US States and Territories 1850: The layer has separate West Virginia and Oklahoma features. In 1850 West Virginia was part of Virginia (it became a state in 1863), and Oklahoma was not a state or territory.

Inquiry

Compelling question

How did slavery divide the United States by 1850?

Pick the questions that suit your class. Each one lists the MapMaker tools it uses, linked to how-to videos.

  1. Free states and slave states

    Use the legend to sort the states into free and slave states, then click two states to read when each became free or slave. Where is the dividing line in the East?

    Tools: Legend, how-to video: Explore Layers and Data (opens in a new tab) · Pop-ups, how-to video: Explore Layers and Data (opens in a new tab)

  2. The Missouri Compromise

    Find the Missouri Compromise Line. Which slave state lies mostly north of it, and why does that matter?

    Tools: Zoom, how-to video: Navigating MapMaker (opens in a new tab) · Legend, how-to video: Explore Layers and Data (opens in a new tab)

  3. The internal slave trade

    Follow the Internal Routes of the US Slave Trade. In which states do they start and end, and which way did they run?

    Tools: Map layers, how-to video: Explore Layers and Data (opens in a new tab) · Zoom, how-to video: Navigating MapMaker (opens in a new tab)

  4. Routes to freedom

    Open the Illinois, Indiana, and Ohio bookmark and follow the Underground Railroad routes north from the Ohio River. Where do they lead, and why do many continue to Canada?

    Tools: Bookmarks, how-to video: Navigating MapMaker (opens in a new tab) · Map layers, how-to video: Explore Layers and Data (opens in a new tab)

Answering the compelling question

Students answer with evidence from at least two layers. Some ways to do it: a paragraph, a sketch that marks free and slave states and one route, or a short talk using the map.

Tools: Sketch, how-to video: Sketch on a Map (opens in a new tab)

Student activity

This is what students see on the Word sheet. Download it to edit it, print it, or open it in Google Docs.

Download Word (English) Download Word (Español)

US Slavery and Slave Trade, 1850

Student sheet

Name Date

Big question: How did slavery divide the United States by 1850?

Open the map in MapMaker: US Slavery and Slave Trade, 1850

  1. Free states and slave states Use the legend to find the free states and the slave states. How many of each are there? Where is the line between them in the East?
  2. The Missouri Compromise Find the Missouri Compromise Line. Slavery was banned north of it in the Louisiana Territory. Which slave state lies mostly north of the line?
  3. The internal slave trade Follow the Internal Routes of the US Slave Trade. In which states do the routes start, and where do they end? In which direction were enslaved people forced to move?
  4. Routes to freedom Open the Illinois, Indiana, and Ohio bookmark. Follow the Underground Railroad routes north from the Ohio River. Where do they lead?

Your answer: Answer the big question using evidence from at least two layers on the map. You can write a paragraph, sketch on the map, or both.

Español: Spanish draft for review by a native speaker. Layer names stay in English, as they appear in MapMaker.

Teacher notes

Before class

The layers come from a 1920 atlas, and the pop-ups note that current scholarship may differ. The US 1850 Original Map layer is off when the map opens; it is the scanned source map, useful for comparing with the traced layers.

Answer notes

1. Free states and slave states

16 free states (including Iowa and California) and 15 slave states (Delaware, Maryland, Virginia, North Carolina, South Carolina, Georgia, Florida, Alabama, Mississippi, Louisiana, Texas, Arkansas, Tennessee, Kentucky and Missouri). The map also draws West Virginia separately; count it as part of Virginia. In the East the line runs along the southern border of Pennsylvania (the Mason–Dixon line) and then the Ohio River.

2. The Missouri Compromise

Missouri. It was admitted as a slave state in 1820 even though most of it lies north of 36°30′ North; Maine was admitted as a free state at the same time to keep the Senate balanced (from the layer's notes).

3. The internal slave trade

The routes run from the older slave states of the Upper South, such as Virginia, Maryland and Kentucky, south and west to the Deep South, such as Mississippi, Louisiana and Alabama. Check the exact routes on the map, which follow the 1920 atlas. You can connect this with the spread of cotton growing.

4. Routes to freedom

North across Ohio, Indiana and Illinois to Lake Erie and the Detroit River, at places such as Cleveland, Ashtabula, Toledo and Detroit, and on to Canada (Chatham and Toronto in Ontario, Montreal in Quebec). After the Fugitive Slave Act of 1850, people who had escaped could be seized even in free states, so Canada was safer.

Common misunderstandings

  • “Freedom seekers were safe once they reached a free state.” After the Fugitive Slave Act of 1850 they could be captured in free states, which is why many routes on the map continue to Canada.
  • “The Underground Railroad was a real railroad.” The routes on the map are paths people walked, rode or sailed, with help along the way; the name borrowed railroad words.
  • “Every Northern state banned slavery at the same time.” The pop-ups give a different year for each free state.

Key words

  • free state
  • slave state
  • Missouri Compromise
  • Fugitive Slave Act
  • Underground Railroad
  • freedom seeker
  • abolition

settings.markdown:
Lessons › US History

Civil War Battlefields

See how the United States split in 1861, compare the railroads of the North and the South, and find where the war's battles were fought.

  • Grade8
  • Time45 minutes, or 10–15 per question
  • UnitThe Civil War
  • Student loginNot needed to explore the map

Open in MapMaker (opens in a new tab) Student sheet (Word, English) Hoja del estudiante (Word, español)

Draft: not yet reviewed Content version 0.1.0, updated 2026-10-12.

About this map

Each layer names its source, so you can check where the information comes from.

LayerWhat it showsSource
U.S. Civil War States and Territories (1863)What it shows: States and territories in 1863 in five legend groups: Union free states; Union slave states (border states); slave states that seceded before Fort Sumter, April 1861; slave states that seceded after Fort Sumter; and territories. No pop-up.Source: State boundaries from IPUMS NHGIS, grouped by the MapMaker team
Civil War Battlefield BoundaryWhat it shows: The land each battle covered. Each pop-up gives the battle's name and its size in acres.Source: National Park Service, American Battlefield Protection Program
Civil War Core AreasWhat it shows: The core of each battlefield, where the heaviest fighting took place. Same pop-up as the boundaries.Source: National Park Service, American Battlefield Protection Program
Boundary between Union and ConfederacyWhat it shows: The line between the Union and the Confederacy. No pop-up.Source: Not stated on the layer (hosted by the MapMaker team)
Railroads 1826 to 1863 (static)What it shows: Railroads built by 1863. No pop-up.Source: Jeremy Atack, historical railroad data (ICPSR 36353), prepared by the MapMaker team
Civil War BattlefieldsWhat it shows: Locations of Civil War battles. No pop-up is set up for them in this map.Source: American Battlefield Trust

Bookmarks: none.

Known issues

  • Open 2026-10-12 Civil War Core Areas pop-up: Uses the same text as the boundary layer, so it calls the core area "the battlefield area".
  • Open 2026-10-12 Civil War Battlefields: No pop-up is set up for the battle points in this map, so students can't click them for names and dates.

Inquiry

Compelling question

How did the geography of a divided nation shape the Civil War?

Pick the questions that suit your class. Each one lists the MapMaker tools it uses, linked to how-to videos.

  1. A nation divided

    Use the legend for U.S. Civil War States and Territories (1863) to sort the states: which seceded before Fort Sumter, which after, and which slave states stayed in the Union?

    Tools: Legend, how-to video: Explore Layers and Data (opens in a new tab)

  2. The border states

    Zoom to Washington, D.C. Which states border it? Why did keeping Maryland in the Union matter?

    Tools: Zoom, how-to video: Navigating MapMaker (opens in a new tab) · Legend, how-to video: Explore Layers and Data (opens in a new tab)

  3. Railroads, North and South

    Compare the Railroads 1826 to 1863 layer north and south of the Boundary between Union and Confederacy. Which side had more railroads, and why would that matter in a war?

    Tools: Map layers, how-to video: Explore Layers and Data (opens in a new tab) · Zoom, how-to video: Navigating MapMaker (opens in a new tab)

  4. Where were the battles?

    Zoom to Virginia, then to Maryland and Pennsylvania, and click battlefield boundaries for names and sizes. Where were most battles fought, and which were fought in Union states?

    Tools: Zoom, how-to video: Navigating MapMaker (opens in a new tab) · Pop-ups, how-to video: Explore Layers and Data (opens in a new tab)

Answering the compelling question

Students answer with evidence from at least two layers. Some ways to do it: a paragraph, a sketch of the front line with notes, or bookmarks saved for a short talk.

Tools: Sketch, how-to video: Sketch on a Map (opens in a new tab) · Bookmarks, how-to video: Navigating MapMaker (opens in a new tab)

Student activity

This is what students see on the Word sheet. Download it to edit it, print it, or open it in Google Docs.

Download Word (English) Download Word (Español)

Civil War Battlefields

Student sheet

Name Date

Big question: How did the geography of a divided nation shape the Civil War?

Open the map in MapMaker: Civil War Battlefields

  1. A nation divided Use the legend. Which states left the Union before the attack on Fort Sumter in April 1861? Which left after? Which slave states stayed in the Union?
  2. The border states Zoom to Washington, D.C. Which two states border it? What would have happened to the capital if Maryland had left the Union?
  3. Railroads, North and South Compare the railroads north and south of the boundary between the Union and the Confederacy. Which side had more? Why would railroads matter in a war?
  4. Where were the battles? Zoom to Virginia, then to Maryland and Pennsylvania. Click two battlefield boundaries. Where were most battles fought? Name a battle fought in a Union state.

Your answer: Answer the big question using evidence from at least two layers on the map. You can write a paragraph, sketch on the map, or both.

Español: Spanish draft for review by a native speaker. Layer names stay in English, as they appear in MapMaker.

Teacher notes

Before class

The map has no bookmarks, so students zoom to Virginia, Washington, D.C., Maryland and Pennsylvania themselves. The battle points have no pop-ups in this map; the battlefield boundary pop-ups carry the names.

Answer notes

1. A nation divided

GroupStates on the map
Seceded before Fort Sumter (7)States on the map: South Carolina, Mississippi, Florida, Alabama, Georgia, Louisiana, Texas
Seceded after Fort Sumter (4)States on the map: Virginia, Arkansas, North Carolina, Tennessee
Union slave states, the border states (5)States on the map: Delaware, Maryland, Kentucky, Missouri, West Virginia
Union free states (19)States on the map: Maine, New Hampshire, Vermont, Massachusetts, Rhode Island, Connecticut, New York, New Jersey, Pennsylvania, Ohio, Indiana, Illinois, Michigan, Wisconsin, Minnesota, Iowa, Kansas, California, Oregon

West Virginia split from Virginia and joined the Union as a state in June 1863, which is why it appears on this 1863 map.

2. The border states

Maryland and Virginia. Virginia joined the Confederacy, so if Maryland had seceded, the Union capital would have been surrounded by Confederate states.

3. Railroads, North and South

The North had a much denser railroad network, so it could move soldiers, food and weapons faster and farther. The map shows lines, not mileage; for figures, use the 1860 census.

4. Where were the battles?

Most battlefields on the map are in the Confederate states, above all Virginia. Antietam (Maryland, 1862) and Gettysburg (Pennsylvania, 1863) were fought in Union states.

Common misunderstandings

  • “All slave states joined the Confederacy.” The legend shows five slave states that stayed in the Union: Delaware, Maryland, Kentucky, Missouri and West Virginia.
  • “The war was fought evenly across the North and the South.” Most battlefields on the map are in Confederate states, above all Virginia.

Key words

  • secession
  • Union
  • Confederacy
  • border state
  • Fort Sumter
  • battlefield
  • railroad network

Standards

CodeStandard
FL SS.8.A.5.4Standard: Identify the division (Confederate and Union States, Border states, western territories) of the United States at the outbreak of the Civil War
TX 8.10(A)Standard: Locate places and regions directly related to major eras and turning points in the United States during the 17th, 18th, and 19th centuries
TX 8.10(C)Standard: Analyze the effects of physical and human geographic factors such as weather, landforms, waterways, transportation, and communication on major historical events in the United States
C3 D2.Geo.2.6-8Standard: Use maps, satellite images, photographs, and other representations to explain relationships between the locations of places and regions, and changes in their environmental characteristics
C3 D2.His.14.6-8Standard: Explain multiple causes and effects of events and developments in the past

settings.markdown:
Lessons › US History

The Battle of Vicksburg

Follow Grant's 1863 march to Vicksburg along the Mississippi River, and see why taking the city split the Confederacy in two.

  • Grade8
  • Time45 minutes, or 10–15 per question
  • UnitThe Civil War
  • Student loginNot needed to explore the map

Open in MapMaker (opens in a new tab) Student sheet (Word, English) Hoja del estudiante (Word, español)

Draft: not yet reviewed Content version 0.1.0, updated 2026-10-12.

About this map

Each layer names its source, so you can check where the information comes from.

LayerWhat it showsSource
Key Places in the Union March to VicksburgWhat it shows: Places on Grant's route in spring 1863, labeled on the map: Miliken's Bend, New Carthage, Hard Times, Bruinsburg Bend and Edwards. No pop-ups.Source: Placed by the MapMaker team
Railroads 1826 to 1911What it shows: Railroads built from 1826 to 1911, so it includes lines built after the war. No pop-up.Source: Jeremy Atack, historical railroad data (ICPSR 36353), prepared by the MapMaker team
Civil War Battlefields (off when the map opens)What it shows: Civil War battles. Each pop-up gives the battle's name, dates and a picture.Source: American Battlefield Trust

Bookmarks: The Battle of Vicksburg.

Known issues

  • Open 2026-10-12 Key Places in the Union March to Vicksburg: The label "Miliken's Bend" is usually spelled Milliken's Bend, and the point at Vicksburg itself is titled "Point".

Inquiry

Compelling question

Why did the Union need Vicksburg, and how did Grant take it?

Pick the questions that suit your class. Each one lists the MapMaker tools it uses, linked to how-to videos.

  1. Why Vicksburg?

    Open The Battle of Vicksburg bookmark. Look at where Vicksburg sits on the Mississippi River and where the railroad leads east. Why would both sides want the city?

    Tools: Bookmarks, how-to video: Navigating MapMaker (opens in a new tab) · Zoom, how-to video: Navigating MapMaker (opens in a new tab)

  2. Grant's route

    Find the key places and put them in order along Grant's route: Milliken's Bend, New Carthage, Hard Times, Bruinsburg Bend, then Edwards. Measure the distance from Milliken's Bend to Bruinsburg Bend.

    Tools: Zoom, how-to video: Navigating MapMaker (opens in a new tab) · Measure, how-to video: Measure with MapMaker (opens in a new tab)

  3. The battles of May 1863

    Turn on Civil War Battlefields and click the battles between Bruinsburg and Vicksburg. Put them in order by date.

    Tools: Map layers, how-to video: Explore Layers and Data (opens in a new tab) · Pop-ups, how-to video: Explore Layers and Data (opens in a new tab)

  4. Splitting the Confederacy

    Zoom out to see the whole Mississippi River. After Vicksburg surrendered on July 4, 1863, which Confederate states were cut off from the rest?

    Tools: Zoom, how-to video: Navigating MapMaker (opens in a new tab)

Answering the compelling question

Students answer with evidence from at least two places on the map. Some ways to do it: a paragraph, Grant's route sketched on the map, or bookmarks saved for a short talk.

Tools: Sketch, how-to video: Sketch on a Map (opens in a new tab) · Bookmarks, how-to video: Navigating MapMaker (opens in a new tab)

Student activity

This is what students see on the Word sheet. Download it to edit it, print it, or open it in Google Docs.

Download Word (English) Download Word (Español)

The Battle of Vicksburg

Student sheet

Name Date

Big question: Why did the Union need Vicksburg, and how did Grant take it?

Open the map in MapMaker: The Battle of Vicksburg

  1. Why Vicksburg? Open The Battle of Vicksburg bookmark. Find Vicksburg on the Mississippi River. Where does the railroad from Vicksburg lead? Why would both sides want the city?
  2. Grant's route Find Milliken's Bend, New Carthage, Hard Times, Bruinsburg Bend and Edwards. Which side of the river is each on? Why did Grant march south before crossing the river? Measure the distance from Milliken's Bend to Bruinsburg Bend: miles
  3. The battles of May 1863 Turn on the Civil War Battlefields layer. Click the battles between Bruinsburg and Vicksburg and list them in order by date.
  4. Splitting the Confederacy Zoom out to see the whole Mississippi River. Vicksburg surrendered on July 4, 1863. Which Confederate states were cut off west of the river?

Your answer: Answer the big question using evidence from at least two places on the map. You can write a paragraph, sketch on the map, or both.

Español: Spanish draft for review by a native speaker. Layer and bookmark names stay in English, as they appear in MapMaker.

Teacher notes

Before class

Civil War Battlefields is off when the map opens. The railroad layer shows lines built up to 1911, so some did not exist in 1863. The key places have labels but no pop-ups.

Answer notes

1. Why Vicksburg?

Vicksburg stands on high bluffs over a bend in the Mississippi, so its guns controlled traffic on the river. A railroad ran east to Jackson, linking the river to the rest of the Confederacy. Whoever held Vicksburg controlled the river between the Confederacy's eastern and western states.

2. Grant's route

Milliken's Bend, New Carthage and Hard Times are on the Louisiana (west) side; Bruinsburg Bend and Edwards are in Mississippi. Vicksburg's guns and the swamps north of the city made a direct attack too hard, so Grant marched south down the Louisiana side and crossed the river at Bruinsburg on April 30, 1863, then turned northeast. Milliken's Bend to Bruinsburg Bend is about 33 miles (53 km) in a straight line.

3. The battles of May 1863

BattleDates
Port GibsonDates: May 1, 1863
RaymondDates: May 12, 1863
Jackson, MississippiDates: May 14, 1863
Champion HillDates: May 16, 1863
Big Black River BridgeDates: May 17, 1863
VicksburgDates: May 18 – July 4, 1863

Grand Gulf (April 29, 1863) was the Union navy's failed attack just before the crossing at Bruinsburg.

4. Splitting the Confederacy

Texas, Arkansas and most of Louisiana. After Port Hudson, Louisiana, surrendered on July 9, 1863, the Union controlled the whole river.

Common misunderstandings

  • “Grant attacked Vicksburg straight across the river.” The key places show he marched south on the Louisiana side and crossed at Bruinsburg, well south of the city.
  • “Vicksburg fell in a single battle.” Its pop-up gives May 18 to July 4, 1863: a siege of about six weeks.
  • “Gettysburg was the only turning point of July 1863.” Vicksburg surrendered on July 4, 1863, the day after Gettysburg ended, and gave the Union the Mississippi.

Key words

  • siege
  • campaign
  • bluff
  • gunboat
  • supply line
  • surrender

Standards

CodeStandard
FL SS.8.A.5.1Standard: Explain the causes, course, and consequence of the Civil War (sectionalism, slavery, states' rights, balance of power in the Senate)
TX 8.10(C)Standard: Analyze the effects of physical and human geographic factors such as weather, landforms, waterways, transportation, and communication on major historical events in the United States
C3 D2.Geo.2.6-8Standard: Use maps, satellite images, photographs, and other representations to explain relationships between the locations of places and regions, and changes in their environmental characteristics
C3 D2.His.14.6-8Standard: Explain multiple causes and effects of events and developments in the past
